proposals.relationship: De Certeau praises Bourdieu’s descriptions of practical ingenuity but questions whether habitus and structural reproduction suppress the tactical inventiveness they reveal.
proposals.evidence_note: Chapter IV, selected English pp. 50, 55–57, 59–60. This is de Certeau’s critical reading, including admiration for the descriptions, not a settled verdict on all Bourdieu. Complete books and original French remain unread for this audit.

proposals.relationship: With Frederick Cooper, Brubaker questions Hall’s claim that identity remains analytically indispensable and proposes more differentiated terms for identification and group formation.
proposals.evidence_note: Beyond Identity, pp. 8–9. The jointly authored criticism explicitly recognizes Hall’s sophisticated anti-essentialism; it does not characterize him as a simple essentialist or deny the political legitimacy of identity claims. Cooper retains equal authorship. One joint argument is projected here, not two independent studies.

proposals.relationship: With Frederick Cooper, Brubaker argues that Omi and Winant’s sharp ethnic/racial-group distinction insufficiently accommodates historical racialization of European immigrants and subsequent changes in racial categories.
proposals.evidence_note: Beyond Identity, p. 40 note 28, specifically discussing Omi and Winant’s 1994 formulation. The authors acknowledge its constructivist definition but challenge this distinction; the edge is not a verdict on every racial-formation historian. Their cited historical studies were not independently reread. Cooper retains equal authorship.

proposals.relationship: Arendt challenges Marx’s elevation of labor and conflation of labor with work, identifying a tension between labor as distinctively human and emancipation from necessity.
proposals.evidence_note: The Human Condition, selected pp. 79, 85–86, 88, 101–104 in the 1998 second edition. The argument dates to 1958. Arendt’s respect for Marx and recognition of labor-power analysis qualify this particular criticism; cited Marx originals were not independently collated.

proposals.relationship: Butler argues that Foucault’s presentation of Herculine Barbin romanticizes pleasures outside power, conflicting with his own account of sexuality’s historical production.
proposals.evidence_note: Gender Trouble, chapter III ii, 1999-edition pp. 119–120, 122–126. This is a specific immanent criticism alongside productive use of Foucault, not rejection of his entire project. Barbin’s memoir and Foucault originals were not newly read; this edition’s pagination is not silently assigned to the 1990 original.

proposals.relationship: Ginzburg questions Foucault’s privileging of exclusion over excluded people, arguing that hostile or distorted records can still support inquiry into subordinate culture.
proposals.evidence_note: The Cheese and the Worms, preface to the Italian edition, pp. xvii–xix in the English translation. Ginzburg credits the attention to exclusion before criticizing the Pierre Riviere collection’s refusal of interpretation. This is his attributed reading; the French originals and collection were not independently collated. John and Anne Tedeschi share translation credit.

proposals.relationship: Agamben proposes to correct or complete Foucault’s biopolitics by placing bare life’s sovereign exclusion in an older political structure and treating its generalized exception as distinctive of modernity.
proposals.evidence_note: Homo Sacer introduction, reformatted English digital pp. 10–13, especially p. 12. This is a theoretical corrective, not a proven universal historical sequence. The author explicitly disavows flattening the historical differences between democracy and totalitarianism. This differs from the existing Foucault-to-Agamben methodological resource. Stanford print pagination and full originals were not collated.

proposals.relationship: Adorno questions Benjamin’s weighting of autonomous and technologically reproduced art, arguing that both contain domination and possibilities of change rather than assigning emancipation to mass reception alone.

Adorno acknowledges their common materialist aims and Benjamin’s contribution while criticizing this weighting. Letter date is not the English collection publication date. The complete correspondence, Benjamin essay and following 1938 letter were not newly collated.

proposals.relationship: Spivak questions Deleuze’s account of oppressed subjects speaking transparently for themselves, insisting that representation and the international division of labour cannot be bypassed.
